   239	\begin{remark}[Asymptotic reading of the distance relations]\label{rem:asymptotic-distance}
   240		Definitions~\ref{def:state-distance}, \ref{def:consistency}, and \ref{def:povm-distance} are asymptotic: every $\approx_\delta$ and $\simeq_\delta$ statement refers to families of states and measurement families indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and the $O(\cdot)$ is taken as $n \to \infty$. None of these relations is a pointwise inequality with an explicit constant. By contrast, the corresponding relations used in the low individual degree chapters (Definitions~\ref{def:simeq} and~\ref{def:approx_delta}) carry no hidden constant. Any explicit quantitative version of the present relations therefore retains the constants absorbed into the $O(\cdot)$; for instance, the triangle inequality of Lemma~\ref{fact:triangle} carries a factor $2$ inside the $O(\cdot)$.
   241	\end{remark}

   245	\begin{lemma}[Consistency versus closeness; Facts 4.13 and 4.14 in \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}]\label{fact:agreement}
   246		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.opFamilyDistSq_le_two_mul_consistencyDefect, MIPStarRE.QPBT.consistencyDefect_le_opFamilyDistSq_of_projective, MIPStarRE.QPBT.consistencyDefect_le_sqrt_of_projective_left}
   247		\leanok

   249		For POVMs $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$, the following hold.
   250		\begin{enumerate}
   251			\item If $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$, then $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$.
   252			\item If $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$ \emph{and} $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are projective measurements, then $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$.
   253			\item If $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$ and either $\{A^x_a\}$ or $\{B^x_a\}$ is a projective measurement, then $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_{\delta^{1/2}} \Id_A \ot B^x_a$.

   255	\end{lemma}
   256	\begin{proof}
   257		Stated in the source without proof; these are Facts 4.13 and 4.14 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. When both families are projective the two operator inequalities hold with equality, so the expansion equals exactly twice the off-diagonal mass; reading this identity in the other direction gives the second item. For the third item, write the off-diagonal mass $\sum_{a \ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^x_b \ket{\psi}$ as an inner product involving $(A^x_a \ot \Id - \Id \ot B^x_a)\ket{\psi}$, using projectivity of one of the two families, and apply the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality; this route costs a square root in the error.

   260	\begin{lemma}[Fact 4.20 in \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}]\label{fact:add-a-proj}
   261		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.opFamilyDistSq_mul_left_le}
   262		\leanok
   263		\uses{def:povm-distance}
   264		Let $\mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mathcal C$ be finite sets, and let $\mu$ be a distribution over question pairs $(x,y)$. Let $\{A^x_{a,\,b}\}$ and $\{B^x_{a,\,b}\}$ be operators whose outcomes range over the product set $\mathcal A \times \mathcal B$. Suppose a set of operators $\{C^y_{a,\,c}\}$, whose outcomes range over the product set $\mathcal A \times \mathcal C$, satisfies the condition $\sum_c (C^y_{a,\,c})^\dagger C^y_{a,\,c} \le \Id$ for all $a$ and all $y$. If $A^x_{a,\,b} \approx_\delta B^x_{a,\,b}$ on average over $x$ sampled from the corresponding marginal of the distribution $\mu$, then $C^y_{a,\,c} A^x_{a,\,b} \approx_\delta C^y_{a,\,c} B^x_{a,\,b}$ on average over $(x,y)$ sampled from $\mu$.
   265	\end{lemma}
   266	\begin{proof}
   267		Fix questions $x, y$ and answers $a \in \mathcal A$, $b \in \mathcal B$. Then
   268		\begin{align*}
   269			\sum_c \bigl\lVert (C^y_{a,\,c} A^x_{a,\,b} - C^y_{a,\,c} B^x_{a,\,b})\, \ket{\psi} \bigr\rVert^2
   270			&= \bra{\psi} (A^x_{a,\,b} - B^x_{a,\,b})^\dagger \Bigl( \sum_c (C^y_{a,\,c})^\dagger C^y_{a,\,c} \Bigr) (A^x_{a,\,b} - B^x_{a,\,b}) \ket{\psi}\\
   271			&\le \bigl\lVert (A^x_{a,\,b} - B^x_{a,\,b})\, \ket{\psi} \bigr\rVert^2\,,
   272		\end{align*}
   273		where the inequality uses the assumption $\sum_c (C^y_{a,\,c})^\dagger C^y_{a,\,c} \le \Id$. Summing over $a, b$ and averaging over $(x,y) \sim \mu$ yields the conclusion.
   274	\end{proof}

   356	\begin{lemma}[Approximate commutation from joint consistency]\label{lem:commutation-analysis}

   361		\begin{align*}
   362			A^x_{a,\,b} \ot \Id_B &\approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_{a,\,b}\,,\\
   363			C^x_{a,\,c} \ot \Id_B &\approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_{a,\,c}\,,
   364		\end{align*}
   365		where $B^x_{a,\,b} = \sum_c B^x_{a,\,b,\,c}$ and $B^x_{a,\,c} = \sum_b B^x_{a,\,b,\,c}$ are the marginals of Definition~\ref{def:povm-conventions}. Then the following approximate commutation relation holds:
   366		\[
   367			[A^x_{a,\,b},\, C^x_{a,\,c}] \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta 0\,.
   368		\]
   369	\end{lemma}

   371		\uses{fact:add-a-proj, fact:triangle}
   372		Applying Lemma~\ref{fact:add-a-proj} to $C^x_{a,\,c} \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_{a,\,c}$ with the multiplier family $\{A^x_{a,\,b} \ot \Id_B\}$, we have
   373		\begin{equation}\label{eq:commutation-analysis-1}
   374			A^x_{a,\,b}\, C^x_{a,\,c} \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta A^x_{a,\,b} \ot B^x_{a,\,c}\,.
   375		\end{equation}

   377		\begin{equation}\label{eq:commutation-analysis-2}
   378			A^x_{a,\,b} \ot B^x_{a,\,c} \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_{a,\,c}\, B^x_{a,\,b} = \Id_A \ot B^x_{a,\,b,\,c}\,.
   379		\end{equation}

   381		\begin{equation}\label{eq:commutation-analysis-3}

    75		uniquely as $x = x^S + x^T$ with $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$; we call $x^S$
    76		(resp.\ $x^T$) the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel to $T$} (resp.\
    77		onto $T$ parallel to $S$). The unique linear map $L : V \to V$ with
    78		$x \mapsto x^S$ is the \emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
    79	\end{definition}
    80	
    81	A subspace may have many complementary subspaces: in $\F_2^2$, the subspace
    82	$S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ has the distinct complements
    83	$\mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and $\mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$. Given a basis of $S$,
    84	one may nevertheless single out a \emph{canonical} complement.
    85	
    86	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
    87		\uses{def:register-subspace}
    88		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
    89		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
    90		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
    91		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
    92		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
    93		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
    94		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
    95		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
    96		\[
    97			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
    98		\]
    99		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace.
   100		% Basis-independence made explicit here: the source defines F^perp through
   101		% a basis but does not assert dependence on it; uniqueness of the reduced
   102		% row echelon form gives dependence on span(F) alone.
   103		Although defined through the basis $F$, it depends only on
   104		$\mathrm{span}(F)$ and the ambient standard basis: two bases of the same
   105		subspace form the rows of row-equivalent matrices, which have the same
   106		reduced row echelon form and hence the same pivot set $J$. The presentation
   107		through Gaussian elimination, adopted by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, makes the
   108		canonical complement efficiently computable. If $S$ is a register subspace
   109		spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the canonical complement of
   110		$\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its span coincides with
   111		$S^\perp$.
   112	\end{definition}
   113	
   114	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   115		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   116		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   117		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   118		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   119		\[
   120			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   121		\]
   122	\end{lemma}
   123	\begin{proof}
   124		\uses{def:canonical-complement}
   125		Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the $v_i$ and
   126		write $A = UB$ with $U$ invertible and $B$ in reduced row echelon form, so
   127		that the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span $S$. The restrictions
   128		of the rows of $B$ to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   129		span $\F^m$, so for every $u \in V$ there is $v \in S$ that agrees with $u$
   130		on the coordinates in $J$. The difference $u - v$ is then supported on the
   131		coordinates outside $J$, that is, $u - v \in T$, which proves $S + T = V$.
   132		Counting dimensions forces $S \cap T = \{0\}$.
   133	\end{proof}
   134	
   135	\begin{definition}[Canonical linear map with prescribed kernel]\label{def:cl-canonical}
   136		\uses{def:canonical-complement, lem:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   137		Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors and let
   138		$F^\perp$ be its canonical complement. The \emph{canonical linear map
   139		$L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ with kernel basis $F$} is the projector onto $T$
   140		parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and
   141		$T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$; this is well defined by
   142		Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement}. Since the canonical complement
   143		depends only on $\mathrm{span}(F)$
   144		(Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}), so does $L$, and we also call
   145		it the \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$}. Note that
   146		$\ker(L) = S$.
   147	\end{definition}
   148	
   149	\begin{definition}[The map $L^\perp$]\label{def:Lperp}
   150		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.canonicalProjPerp}
   151		\leanok
   152		\uses{def:cl-canonical, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   153		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map and let $F$ be a basis for
   154		$\ker(L)^\perp$. Define $L^\perp : V \to V$ as the canonical linear map with
   155		kernel basis $F$. (By the basis-independence noted in
   156		Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}, the map $L^\perp$ depends only
   157		on $\ker(L)$ and not on the chosen basis $F$.)
   158	\end{definition}
   159	
   160	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:L_perp_perp}
   161		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.ker_canonicalProjPerp}
   162		\leanok
   163		\uses{def:Lperp}
   164		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map, $F$ a basis for
   165		$\ker(L)^\perp$, and $L^\perp$ as in Definition~\ref{def:Lperp}. Then
   166		$\ker(L^\perp) = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   167	\end{lemma}
   168	\begin{proof}
   169		\uses{def:Lperp, def:cl-canonical, lem:canonical-complement}
   170		Set $S = \mathrm{span}(F) = \ker(L)^\perp$ and $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$;
   171		by Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement} every $v \in V$ decomposes uniquely
   172		as $v = v^S + v^T$, and by definition $L^\perp v = v^T$. If
   173		$L^\perp v = 0$ then $v = v^S \in S = \ker(L)^\perp$. Conversely, if
   174		$v \in S$ then $v^T = 0$, so $L^\perp v = 0$.
   175	\end{proof}

   177	\section{Finite fields, traces, and self-dual bases}
   178	% Paper labels sec:finite-fields, sec:subfields, sec:ff-representations kept
   179	% for cross-reference fidelity.
   180	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   181	\label{sec:subfields}

   184	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ a prime power. We write $\F_p$ and $\F_q$ for
   185	the finite fields with $p$ and $q$ elements; $p$ is the characteristic of
   186	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.
   187	
   188	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   189		% The source lets k range over all integers; the extension field exists
   190		% only for k >= 1, so that domain condition is made explicit here.
   191		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a
   192		subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of dimension $k$
   193		over $\F_q$.
   194		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   195		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   196		\[
   197			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad
   198			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   199		\]
   200		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   201		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   202		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   203		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   204		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   205		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   206		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   207		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   208		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for
   209		$M = (M_{i,j}) \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ let
   210		$\chi_q(M) \in \Mat_{mk,nk}(\F_q)$ be the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th
   211		block is $K_{M_{i,j}}$; and for a set $S$ of vectors put
   212		$\kappa_q(S) = \{\kappa_q(v) : v \in S\}$. When $q = p$ is the field
   213		characteristic, the subscript is omitted and we write $\kappa$ and $\chi$.
   214	\end{definition}
   215	
   216	\begin{definition}[Admissible field size]\label{def:admissible-size}
   217		A field size $q$ is \emph{admissible} if $q = 2^k$ for an odd integer $k$.
   218	\end{definition}
   219	
   220	Only fields $\F_{2^k}$ with $k$ odd are used in the analysis of the Pauli basis
   221	test.
   222	
   223	\begin{definition}[Trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$]\label{def:subfield-trace}
   224		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size}
   225		The \emph{trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$} is the map
   226		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   227		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   228			\tr_{q^k \to q} : a \mapsto \Tr(K_a)
   229		\end{equation}
   230		for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $K_a$ is the multiplication table of $a$ with
   231		respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$. The trace is an $\F_q$-linear map from
   232		$\F_{q^k}$ to $\F_q$, and it is independent of the choice of basis, as can
   233		be seen from the equivalent formula
   234		\[
   235			\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   236		\]
   237		For admissible $q = 2^k$ we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q \to 2}$.
   238	\end{definition}
   239	
   240	\begin{definition}[Dual, self-dual, and normal bases]\label{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   241		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.IsDualBasisPair, MIPStarRE.QPBT.Basis.IsSelfDual, MIPStarRE.QPBT.Basis.IsNormal, MIPStarRE.QPBT.exists_selfDualNormalBasis}
   242		\leanok
   243		\uses{def:subfield-trace}
   244		A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', \dots, e_k'\}$ of a basis
   245		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$ is a basis such that
   246		$\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for all
   247		$i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$. A \emph{self-dual basis} is one equal to its own
   248		dual. If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set
   249		$\{\alpha^{q^j}\}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$, that
   250		basis is called a \emph{normal basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not
   251		exist for every field extension, but for $q = 2$ and odd $k$ a self-dual
   252		normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ always exists; \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}
   253		exhibits one through an explicit construction.
   254	\end{definition}

   256	\begin{lemma}[Coordinate maps of self-dual bases]\label{lem:downsize_field}
   257		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.basisCoord_apply_eq_trace, MIPStarRE.QPBT.trace_mul_eq_dotProduct_basisCoord, MIPStarRE.QPBT.chi_mulVec_basisCoord}
   258		\leanok
   259		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace,
   260			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   261		Let $q$ be a prime power, $k \ge 1$ an integer, and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual
   262		basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The map $\kappa_q$ corresponding to
   263		$\{e_i\}$ satisfies:
   264		\begin{enumerate}
   265			\item for all $x \in \F_{q^k}$,
   266			      $\kappa_q(x) = \bigl(\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_1), \dots,
   267			      \tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_k)\bigr)$;
   268			\item for all $x, y \in \F_{q^k}$,
   269			      $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \kappa_q(x) \cdot \kappa_q(y)$;
   270			\item for all $M \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in \F_{q^k}^n$,
   271			      $\chi_q(M)\, \kappa_q(v) = \kappa_q(Mv)$.
   272		\end{enumerate}
   273		Items 1 and 2 use self-duality; item 3 holds for an arbitrary basis.
   274	\end{lemma}
   275	\begin{proof}
   276		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   277		For item 1, write $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$, multiply both sides by $e_j$, and
   278		take traces: $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j)
   279		= x_j$ by self-duality. For item 2, expand
   280		$xy = \sum_{i,j} x_i y_j e_i e_j$ and take traces; self-duality retains
   281		exactly the diagonal terms, giving $\sum_i x_i y_i = \kappa_q(x) \cdot
   282		\kappa_q(y)$. For item 3, the $i$-th block of $\kappa_q(Mv)$ equals
   283		$\sum_j \kappa_q(M_{i,j} v_j) = \sum_j K_{M_{i,j}}\, \kappa_q(v_j)$, which
   284		is the $i$-th block row of $\chi_q(M)$ applied to $\kappa_q(v)$.
   285	\end{proof}

   287	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:one}
   288		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.trace_basis_eq_one_of_selfDual_normal, MIPStarRE.QPBT.basisCoord_one_of_selfDual_normal}
   289		\leanok

   293		representation $\kappa(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all-ones

   451	\section{Lines}
   452	
   453	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of
   454	the Pauli basis test (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}) sample lines in $\F_q^m$;
   455	we record here the definition of lines and their canonical representatives.
   456	
   457	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   458		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   459		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   460		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   461			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   462		\end{equation}
   463		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   464		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   465		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   466		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   467		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   468		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   469		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   470		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   471	\end{definition}
   472	
   473	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   474		\uses{def:line}
   475		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   476		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   477	\end{proposition}
   478	\begin{proof}
   479		\uses{def:line}
   480		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   481		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   482		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   483		inclusion.
   484	\end{proof}
   485	
   486	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   487	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   488	representation is obtained as follows.
   489	
   490	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]\label{def:line-representative}
   491		\uses{def:line, def:cl-canonical, prop:line-equiv}
   492		Let $\ell$ be a line in direction $v \neq 0$, and let
   493		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v : \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with
   494		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$
   495		(Definition~\ref{def:cl-canonical}). The \emph{canonical representative of
   496		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   497		\[
   498			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   499		\]
   500		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   501		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with
   502		$u_0$ in the image, so $u_0 = u - tv \in \ell$ and
   503		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u_0) = u_0$; moreover any two points of $\ell$ differ by
   504		a multiple of $v$ and therefore have the same image under
   505		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$. A line $\ell = \ell(u,v)$ is henceforth canonically
   506		represented by the pair $(u_0, v)$. (For $v = 0$, where the singleton
   507		$\{u\}$ leaves no independent kernel basis, we take $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_0$ to
   508		be the identity---the canonical linear map with empty kernel basis---so
   509		that $u_0 = u$; the source leaves this case implicit.)
   510	\end{definition}

   512	\section{Quantum registers and EPR states}
   513	% Paper label sec:lin-reg kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   514	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   515	
   516	\begin{definition}[State space of a linear register]\label{def:lin-reg}
   517		\uses{def:complementary}
   518		For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension
   519		$|V|$, endowed with the canonical orthonormal basis
   520		$\{\ket{x}\}_{x \in V}$. A \emph{quantum state on $V$} is a unit vector
   521		$\ket{\psi}_V \in \C^V$. If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_i$ is a direct sum of
   522		subspaces over $\F$, then $\C^V$ is identified with
   523		$\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{V_i}$ by identifying
   524		$\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus x_k}$ with
   525		$\ket{x_1} \ot \dots \ot \ket{x_k}$. In particular, a basis $\{e_i\}$ of
   526		$V$ yields the decomposition $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k (\F e_i)$ and hence
   527		$\C^V = \bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{|\F|}$; the factors $\C^{|\F|}$ are called
   528		the \emph{qudits} of $\C^V$.
   529	\end{definition}
   530	
   531	\begin{definition}[EPR state]\label{def:EPR}
   532		\uses{def:lin-reg}
   533		For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, the \emph{EPR state} on
   534		$\C^V \ot \C^V$ is
   535		\[
   536			\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}_V
   537			= \frac{1}{\sqrt{|V|}} \sum_{x \in V} \ket{x} \ot \ket{x}\;.
   538		\]
   539		We write $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ for $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}_{\F_q}$ and
   540		$\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}$ for $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$.
   541	\end{definition}

   543	\section{Generalized Pauli observables}
   544	% Paper label sec:generalized-pauli kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   545	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
   546	
   547	\begin{definition}[Generalized Pauli observables]\label{def:generalized-pauli}
   548		\uses{def:subfield-trace, def:lin-reg}
   549		Let $p$ be a prime and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$. The \emph{generalized Pauli
   550		observables over $\F_p$} are the unitaries on $\C^{\F_p}$ given by
   551		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-fp}
   552			\sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   553			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   554			\sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \omega^{bj} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   555		\end{equation}
   556		for $a, b \in \F_p$, with arithmetic over $\F_p$. For $q = p^k$, the
   557		\emph{generalized Pauli observables over $\F_q$} are the unitaries on
   558		$\C^{\F_q}$
   559		\[
   560			\tau^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   561			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   562			\tau^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \omega^{\tr(bj)} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   563		\]
   564		for $a, b \in \F_q$, where $\tr$ here denotes $\tr_{q \to p}$
   565		(Definition~\ref{def:subfield-trace}); for admissible $q$ this agrees with
   566		the standing shorthand, $p = 2$, and $\omega = -1$, so that all phases are
   567		signs. All the $\tau^X$ operators commute with one another, as do all the
   568		$\tau^Z$ operators. Their common eigenbases consist of the vectors
   569		$\ket{e_W}$, labeled by $e \in \F_q$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
   570		\[
   571			\ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{j \in \F_q}
   572			\omega^{-\tr(ej)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
   573			\ket{e_Z} = \ket{e}\;;
   574		\]
   575		the Fourier transform
   576		\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourier-f}
   577			F = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b \in \F_q}
   578			\omega^{-\tr(ab)} \ket{a}\bra{b}
   579		\end{equation}
   580		maps the computational ($Z$) eigenbasis to the $X$ eigenbasis. We write
   581		$\{\tau^W_e\}_{e \in \F_q}$ for the projective measurement whose elements
   582		are the rank-one projectors onto the vectors of the $W$ eigenbasis. For
   583		systems of $n$ qudits, we write, for $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a \in \F_q^n$,
   584		\[
   585			\tau^W(a) = \tau^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \tau^W(a_n)\;, \qquad
   586			\ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}
   587		\]
   588		for $e \in \F_q^n$, with associated rank-one projectors $\tau^W_e$.
   589	\end{definition}
   590	
   591	\begin{lemma}[Product and twisted commutation relations]\label{lem:twisted-commutation}
   592		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.primeTauObservable_mul,
   593			MIPStarRE.QPBT.primeTauObservable_pow,
   594			MIPStarRE.QPBT.primeTauObservable_pow_char,
   595			MIPStarRE.QPBT.primeTauObservable_isUnitary,
   596			MIPStarRE.QPBT.primeTauObservable_eigenvalue_pow_char,
   597			MIPStarRE.QPBT.primeTauObservable_X_mul_Z}
   598		\leanok
   599		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   600		Let $q = p^k$, let $n \ge 1$ be an integer, and let $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   601		\begin{enumerate}
   602			\item For all $a, a' \in \F_q$ and $b \in \F_p$,
   603			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
   604				      \tau^W(a)\, \tau^W(a') = \tau^W(a + a')
   605				      \qquad \text{and} \qquad
   606				      \bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^b = \tau^W(ab)\;;
   607			      \end{equation}
   608			      in particular $\bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^p = \Id$. By the explicit
   609			      definitions each $\tau^W(a)$ is unitary, and its eigenvalues are
   610			      $p$-th roots of unity.
   611			\item For all $a, b \in \F_q^n$,
   612			      % Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   613			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fq}
   614				      \tau^X(a)\, \tau^Z(b)
   615				      = \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^Z(b)\, \tau^X(a)\;,
   616			      \end{equation}
   617			      where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i \in \F_q$. The case
   618			      $q = p$, $n = 1$ reads
   619			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fp}
   620				      \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b)
   621				      = \omega^{-ab}\, \sigma^Z(b)\, \sigma^X(a)
   622				      \qquad \text{for all } a, b \in \F_p\;.
   623			      \end{equation}
   624		\end{enumerate}
   625	\end{lemma}
   626	\begin{proof}
   627		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   628		All identities are verified on computational basis states. For the product
   629		relations with $W = X$, shifting twice by $a'$ and $a$ equals shifting by
   630		$a + a'$; with $W = Z$, the phases $\omega^{\tr(aj)}\omega^{\tr(a'j)}$
   631		combine by $\F_q$-linearity of the trace, and the power relation follows by
   632		iterating. For the scalar twisted commutation,
   633		$\tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$, while
   634		$\tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(b(j+a))}\ket{j + a} =
   635		\omega^{\tr(ab)}\,\omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$. The multi-qudit relation
   636		follows by applying the scalar relation factor by factor and summing the
   637		exponents, using $\tr(a \cdot b) = \sum_i \tr(a_i b_i)$. For $q = p$ the
   638		trace is the identity map, which gives \eqref{eq:twisted-fp}.
   639	\end{proof}
   640	
   641	\begin{lemma}[Fourier cancellation over a subspace]\label{lem:cancellation}
   642		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.ffChar_dotProduct_submodule_expect_eq_zero}
   643		\leanok
   644		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal, def:subfield-trace}
   645		Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_q^k$ and let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$, where
   646		$p$ is the characteristic of $\F_q$ and $\tr = \tr_{q \to p}$. For all
   647		$v \notin V^\perp$,
   648		\[
   649			\E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr(\bu \cdot v)} = 0\;,
   650		\]
   651		where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $\bu$ in $V$.
   652	\end{lemma}
   653	\begin{proof}
   654		This is Fact 3.2 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Since $v \notin V^\perp$,
   655		the $\F_q$-linear functional $u \mapsto u \cdot v$ is not identically zero
   656		on $V$, hence surjective onto $\F_q$; composing with the nonzero map $\tr$
   657		shows that there is $u_0 \in V$ with $\tr(u_0 \cdot v) \neq 0$. Writing $C$
   658		for the expectation, translation invariance of the uniform distribution on
   659		$V$ gives
   660		$C = \E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr((\bu + u_0) \cdot v)}
   661		= \omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)}\, C$, and $\omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)} \neq 1$
   662		forces $C = 0$.
   663	\end{proof}
   664	
   665	\begin{lemma}[Fourier expansion of Pauli observables]\label{lem:pauli-observable-expansion}
   666		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   667		For every integer $n \ge 1$, all $W \in \{X, Z\}$, and all $a \in \F_q^n$,
   668		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   669		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj}
   670			\tau^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \F_q^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^W_b\;,
   671		\end{equation}
   672		and conversely
   673		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
   674			\E_{\ba \sim \F_q^n}\, \omega^{-\tr(\ba \cdot b)}\, \tau^W(\ba)
   675			= \sum_{b' \in \F_q^n} \E_{\ba \sim \F_q^n}\,
   676			\omega^{\tr(\ba \cdot (b' - b))}\, \tau^W_{b'}
   677			= \tau^W_b\;.
   678		\end{equation}
   679	\end{lemma}
   680	\begin{proof}
   681		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, lem:cancellation}
   682		Each $\ket{b_W}$ is an eigenvector of $\tau^W(a)$ with eigenvalue
   683		$\omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}$: for $W = Z$ this is immediate from the
   684		definition, and for $W = X$ it follows from the single-qudit computation
   685		$\tau^X(a)\ket{e_X} = \omega^{\tr(ae)}\ket{e_X}$, applied factor by factor.
   686		Expanding $\tau^W(a)$ in the orthonormal eigenbasis
   687		$\{\ket{b_W}\}_{b \in \F_q^n}$ gives the first display. For the inversion,
   688		substitute the first display and exchange the order of summation; by
   689		Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation} applied with $V = \F_q^n$ (so that
   690		$V^\perp = \{0\}$), the inner expectation vanishes unless $b' = b$, where
   691		it equals $1$.
   692	\end{proof}

   256	
   257	We note that over finite fields, the notion of orthogonality does not possess
   258	all of the same intuitive properties of orthogonality over fields such as $\R$
   259	or $\C$; for example, a non-zero subspace $S$ may be orthogonal to itself (e.g.\
   260	$\mathrm{span} \{ (1,1) \}$ over $\F_2$).
   261	However, the following remains true over all fields.
   262	
   263	\begin{lemma}
   264	  \label{lem:perp_perp}
   265	  Suppose $S$ is a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) =
   266	  \dim(V)$, and 
   267	  \begin{equation*}
   268	    (S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
   269	  \end{equation*}
   270	\end{lemma}
   271	
   272	\begin{proof}
   273	  The statement about the dimensions follows from the fact that vectors in $S^\perp$ are
   274	  the solution to a feasible linear system of equations with $\dim(S)$ linearly
   275	  independent rows; this implies that the solution space has dimension exactly
   276	  $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$.
   277	  Next, we argue that $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   278	  Let $u \in S$.
   279	  Since all vectors $v \in S^\perp$ are orthogonal to every vector in $S$,
   280	  in particular $u$, this implies that $u \in (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   281	  By dimension counting, it follows that $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$.
   282	\end{proof}

   284	\begin{definition}\label{def:complementary}
   285	  Given a linear space $V$, two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of $V$ are said to form a
   286	  pair of \emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
   287	\begin{equation*}
   288	  S \cap T = \{ 0 \}, \quad S + T = V\;.
   289	\end{equation*}
   290	In this case, we write $V = S \oplus T$.
   291	Any $x\in V$ can be written as $x = x^S + x^T$ for $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$
   292	in a unique way.
   293	We refer to $x^S$ (resp.~$x^T$) as the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel
   294	  to $T$} (resp.~\emph{onto $T$ parallel to $S$}).
   295	We call the unique linear map $L: V \to V$ that maps $x \mapsto x^S$ the
   296	\emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
   297	\end{definition}
   298	
   299	A given subspace may have many different complementary subspaces: consider the
   300	example of $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1) \}$ in $\F_2^2$.
   301	Different complementary subspaces include $T = \mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and
   302	$T' = \mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$.
   303	It is convenient to define the notion of a \emph{canonical complement} of a
   304	subspace $S$, given a basis for $S$.
   305	
   306	\begin{definition}
   307	  \label{def:canonical-complement}
   308	  Let $E$ be the standard basis of linear space $V = \F^n$.
   309	  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
   310	  independent vectors in $V$.
   311	  The \emph{canonical complement $F^\perp$ of $F$} is the set of $n-m$ independent
   312	  vectors defined as follows.
   313	  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.
   314		Using a canonical algorithm for Gaussian elimination that works over arbitrary
   315	  fields, transform the $m\times n$ matrix $(a_{i, j})$ to reduced row echelon
   316	  form $(b_{i, j})$.
   317	  Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices of the leading $1$ entry in each row
   318	  of $(b_{i, j})$.
   319	  The canonical complement is defined as $F^\perp = \{ \hat{e}_j : j \not\in J \}$.
   320	\end{definition}
   321	
   322	
   323	\begin{remark}
   324	We emphasize that the canonical complement $F^\perp$ is a \emph{set} (rather than
   325	a subspace), and it is defined with respect to a \emph{set} of linearly
   326	independent vectors $F$. While there are equivalent ways of defining
   327	a canonical complement of a \emph{subspace} in a basis-independent manner, 
   328	we use this particular definition because it makes it clear that
   329	the canonical complement of a set $F$ is efficiently computable. 
   330	\end{remark}
   331	
   332	\begin{remark}
   333	  Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V$.
   334	  Suppose subspace $S$ is a register subspace of $V$ spanned by
   335	  $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$.
   336	  Then it is not hard to verify that the canonical complement of $\hat{E}_{0}$ is
   337	  $\hat{E}\setminus \hat{E}_0$ and the span of the canonical complement coincides with
   338	  $S^\perp$.
   339	\end{remark}
   340	
   341	
   342	\begin{lemma}
   343	  \label{lem:canonical-complement}
   344	  Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors $F = \{v_1,\ldots,v_m \}
   345	  \subseteq V$ and let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$ as defined
   346	  in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   347	  Let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   348	  Then
   349	  \begin{equation*}
   350	   \qquad S + T = V\;,  S \cap T = \{ 0 \} \;.
   351	  \end{equation*}
   352	\end{lemma}
   353	
   354	\begin{proof}
   355	To show the first item, we must show that every vector in $V$ can be
   356	written as a sum of an element of $S$ and an element of $T$. To do
   357	this, let $A = (a_{i, j})$ be the $m\times n$ matrix over $\F$ whose
   358	rows are the vectors $v_i$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   359	  Write $A = U B$ where $U$ is invertible and $B$ is in reduced row echelon
   360	  form.
   361	  Let $J$ be the set of column indices of the leading 1 entries in
   362	  $B$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.  
   363	  Now, the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span the subpsace $S$, and the restriction of
   364	  these rows to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   365	  span $\F^m$. Thus, for any vector $u \in V$, there is some linear
   366	  combination $v$ of rows of $B$ such that $u$ and $v$ agree
   367	  restricted to the columns in $J$. In other words, there exists $v
   368	  \in S$ such that $u_j = v_j$ for all $j \in J$. Hence, $u = v + w$
   369	  for $w \in T$, where $T$ is the canonical complement.
   370	  This shows $S + T = V$.
   371	  Counting dimensions shows that necessarily $S\cap T =
   372	  \{0\}$.
   373	\end{proof}
   374	
   375	\begin{definition}
   376	  \label{def:cl-canonical}
   377	  Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors.
   378	  Let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$.
   379	  Define the \emph{canonical linear map $L \in \End(V)$ with kernel basis $F$}
   380	  as the projector onto $T$ parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and $T
   381	  = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   382	  When the basis $F$ for $S$ is clear from context, we refer to this map as the
   383	  \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$.}
   384	\end{definition}
   385	
   386	\begin{definition}
   387	  \label{def:Lperp}
   388	  Let $L \in \End(V)$ be a linear map, and let $F$ be a basis for
   389	  $\ker(L)^\perp$.
   390	  Define $L^\perp : V \rightarrow V$ as the canonical linear map with kernel
   391	  basis $F$.
   392	\end{definition}
   393	
   394	\begin{lemma}
   395	  \label{lem:L_perp_perp}
   396	  Let $L \in \End(V)$ be a linear map and $F$ a basis for $\ker(L)^\perp$.
   397	  Let $L^\perp \in \End(V)$ be the linear map defined in
   398	  Definition~\ref{def:Lperp}.
   399	  Then $\ker(L^\perp) = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   400	\end{lemma}
   401	
   402	\begin{proof}
   403	  First, to set notation, let $S = \mathrm{span}(F) = \ker(L)^\perp$ and $T =
   404	  \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement},
   405	  any vector $v \in V$ can be uniquely decomposed as $v = v^S +
   406	  v^T$. 
   407	
   408	  Now we will show the lemma.  First we show that if $\ker(L^\perp) \subseteq \ker(L)^\perp$. Let
   409	  $v \in \ker(L^\perp)$, and write $v = v^S + v^T$.  By the definition
   410	  of $L^\perp$, it follows that $v^T = 0$, and hence $v \in S = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   411	
   412	  It remains to show the other direction, that is $\ker(L)^\perp \subseteq
   413	  \ker(L^\perp)$. Let $v \in \ker(L)^\perp = S$. Then $v = v^S + v^T$
   414	  where $v^T = 0$, and hence by the definition of $L^\perp$, $L^\perp
   415	  v = 0$. Hence $v \in \ker(L^\perp)$.
   416	
   417	  
   418	\end{proof}

   420	\subsection{Finite fields}
   421	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   422	
   423	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ be a prime power.
   424	We denote the finite fields of $p$ and $q$ elements by $\Fp$ and $\Fq$
   425	respectively.
   426	The prime $p$ is the characteristic of field $\Fq$, and field $\Fp$ is the
   427	\emph{prime subfield} of $\Fq$.
   428	We sometimes omit the subscript and simply use $\F$ to denote the finite field
   429	when the size of the field is implicit from context.
   430	For general background on finite fields, and explicit algorithms for elementary
   480	
   481	The \emph{trace of\/ $\F_{q^k}$ over\/ $\Fq$} is defined as
   482	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   483	  \tr_{q^k \to q} :\; a \,\mapsto \, \Tr(K_a)
   484	\end{equation}
   485	for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $\Tr(K_a)$ is the trace of the multiplication table
   486	of $a$ with respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$.
   487	By definition, the trace is an $\Fq$-linear map from $\F_{q^k}$ to
   488	$\Fq$. The trace is in fact independent of the choice of basis, which
   489	can be seen from the following equivalent definition~\cite[Definition 2.1.80]{mullen2013handbook}:
   490	\[
   491		\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   492	\]
   493	
   494	A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', e_2', \ldots, e_k' \}$ of $\{e_1, e_2, \ldots,
   495	e_k\}$ is a basis such that $\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for
   496	all $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
   497	A \emph{self-dual basis} is one that is equal to its dual.
   498	If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set $\{ \alpha^{q^j} \}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a
   499	basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\Fq$, the basis is called a \emph{normal
   500	  basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not exist for all fields but are guaranteed to exist under
   501	certain conditions; in particular, if $q = 2$ and $k$ is odd, as will
   502	be shown in \Cref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   503	
   504	We record some convenient facts about the maps $\downsize(\cdot)$ and
   505	$\downsizem(\cdot)$ for self-dual bases.
   506	
   507	\begin{lemma}
   508	  \label{lem:downsize_field}
   509	  Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis for
   510	  $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   511	  The map $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ corresponding to $\{e_i\}$ satisfies the
   512	  following properties:
   513	  \begin{enumerate}
   514	  \item For all $x \in \F_{q^k}$, $\downsize_q(x) = \bigl( \tr_{q^k \to
   515	      q}(xe_1),\ldots,\tr_{q^k \to q}(xe_k) \bigr)$.
   516	  \item For all $x,y \in \F_{q^k}$, $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \downsize_q(x) \cdot
   517	    \downsize_q(y)$.
   518	  \item For all $M \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in
   519	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsizem_q(M) \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(Mv)$.
   520	  \end{enumerate}
   521	\end{lemma}
   522	 
   523	\begin{proof}
   524	  We show each property by direct calculation.
   525	  \begin{enumerate}
   526	    \item Let $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. Then by the definition of
   527	    $\downsize_q$, $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$. Multiplying both sides by $e_j$
   528	    and taking the trace yields $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i
   529	    \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j) = x_j$, where the last equality is by
   530	    self-duality of the basis.
   531	    \item Write $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ and $\downsize_q(y) =
   532	      (y_1, \dots, y_k)$. Then
   533	      \begin{align*}
   534	        \tr_{q^k \to q} (xy) &= \tr_{q^k \to q}(\sum_{ij} x_i y_j e_i
   535	                               e_j) \\
   536	                             &= \sum_{ij} x_i y_j \tr_{q^k \to q}(  e_i
   537	                               e_j) \\
   538	                             &= \downsize_q(x) \cdot \downsize_q(y),
   539	      \end{align*}
   540	      where the last equality uses the self-duality of the basis.
   541	    \item
   542	      We compute the $i$th $\F_q^k$-block of $\downsize_q(Mv)$:
   543	      \begin{align*}
   544	        \downsize_q(Mv)_i &= \sum_{ij} \downsize_q(M_{ij} v_j) \\
   545	                          &= \sum_{ij} K_{M_{ij}} \downsize_q(v_j) \\
   546	                          &= \downsizem_q(M)_{ij} \downsize_q(v_j) ,
   547	      \end{align*}
   548	      where we have applied the definition of the multiplication table
   549	      $K_{M_{ij}}$ and the map $\downsizem_q(\cdot)$.
   550	  \end{enumerate}
   551	\end{proof}
   552	
   553	For $z\in \F^n$ and $V,W$ a pair of complementary subspaces, recall from
   554	Definition~\ref{def:complementary} the notation $z^V$ for the projection of $z$
   555	onto $V$ and parallel to $W$.
   556	
   557	\begin{lemma}
   558	  \label{lem:downsize_subspace}
   559	  Let $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ denote the map corresponding to a
   560	  basis $\{e_i\}$ for $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   561	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_{q^k}^n$ with linearly independent basis
   562	  $\{b_1,\ldots,b_t\} \subseteq \F_{q^k}^n$.
   563	  Then the following hold:
   564	  \begin{enumerate}
   565	 	\item $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace of $\,\F_{q}^{nk}$.
   566		\item $\{ \downsize_q(e_i b_j) \}_{i,j}$ is a linearly independent basis of
   567	    $\downsize_q(V)$ over $\F_q$.
   568		\item Let $V, W$ be complementary subspaces of $\F_{q^k}^n$.
   569	    Then $V' = \downsize_q(V)$ and $W' = \downsize_q(W)$ are complementary
   570	    subspaces of $\F_q^{kn}$, and furthermore for all vectors $z \in
   571	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsize_q(z^V) = \downsize_q(z)^{V'}$ and
   572	    $\downsize_q(z^W) = \downsize_q(z)^{W'}$.
   573	  \end{enumerate}
   574	\end{lemma}
   575	
   576	\begin{proof}
   577	  For the first item, we first verify that $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace.
   578	  Since $V$ is a subspace, it contains $0 \in \F_{q^k}^n$, and therefore $\downsize_q(0)
   579	  = 0$ is also in $\downsize_q(V)$.
   580	  Let $u', v' \in \downsize_q(V)$.
   581	  Using that $\downsize_q$ is a bijection there exist $u,v \in \F_{q^k}^n$ such that
   582	  $u' = \downsize_q(u)$ and $v' = \downsize_q(v)$. Therefore
   583	  \[
   584	    u' + v' = \downsize_q(u) + \downsize_q(v) =
   585	    \downsize_q(u + v) \in \downsize_q(V)\;,
   586	  \]
   587	  where the inclusion follows because $V$ is a subspace and thus contains $u +
   588	  v$.
   589	  Finally, for all $x' \in \F_{q}$, for all $v \in V$, we have that $x'
   590	  \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(x' v)\in \downsize_q(V)$ where we used that $V$
   591	  is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q^k}$ and thus by $\F_q$ (since
   592	  $\F_q$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$).
   593	  Thus $\downsize_q(V)$ is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q}$.
   594	
   595	  For the second item, note that an element $v \in V$ can be expressed uniquely
   596	  as $v = \sum_{i = 1}^t v_i b_i$ for $v_i \in \F_{q^k}$.
   597	  The element $v_i$ can further be written as $\sum_j v_{i, j} e_j$ where $v_{i,
   598	    j} \in \F_q$.
   599	  Thus $v$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ e_j b_i \}$, and therefore
   600	  $\downsize_q(v)$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ \downsize_q (e_j
   601	  b_i) \}$.
   602	  To establish that the vectors $\{ \downsize_q(e_j b_i) \}$ are linearly
   603	  independent, suppose towards contradiction that they are not.
   604	  Then there would exist $\alpha_{i, j} \in \F_q$ such that at least one
   605	  $\alpha_{i, j}$ is nonzero and
   606	  \begin{align*}
   607	    0 & = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_{i, j} \downsize_q(e_j b_i) \\
   608	      & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \bigl (\sum_j \alpha_{i, j}
   609	        e_j \bigr) b_i \Bigr) \\
   610	      & = \downsize_q \left ( \sum_i \beta_i b_i \right ),
   611	  \end{align*}
   612	  where we define $\beta_i = \sum_j \alpha_{i, j} e_j$.
   613	  Since at least one $\alpha_{i, j} \neq 0$ and the $\{e_j\}$ are linearly
   614	  independent over $\F_q$, there exists $i$ such that $\beta_i \neq 0$, which
   615	  means that there is a non-trivial linear combination of the basis elements
   616	  $b_i$ that equals $0$ under $\downsize_q(\cdot)$.
   617	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is injective, we get a contradiction with linear
   618	  independence of the $\{b_i\}$.
   619	
   620	  For the third item, we observe that $\downsize_q(V)$ and $\downsize_q(W)$ must
   621	  be complementary because $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a linear map as well as a
   622	  bijection.
   623	  Let $\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}$ and $\{v_{m+1},\ldots,v_n\}$ denote bases for $V$ and
   624	  $W$, respectively.
   625	  Thus the set $\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$ forms a basis for $\F_{q^k}^n$, and from the
   626	  previous item, the set $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{i,\, j}$ is a basis for
   627	  $\F_q^{kn}$.
   628	  Furthermore, the sets $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{j,\,i = 1,\ldots m}$ and
   629	  $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{j,\, i = m+1,\ldots n}$ are bases for
   630	  $\downsize_q(V)$ and $\downsize_q(W)$, respectively.
   631	
   632	  There is a unique choice of coefficients $\alpha_{i, j} \in \F_q$ such that
   633	  $\downsize_q(z) = \sum_{i, j} \alpha_{i, j} \downsize_q(e_j v_i)$.
   634	  But then
   635	  \begin{align*}
   636	    \downsize_q(z) & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \bigl ( \sum_j
   637	                     \alpha_{i, j} e_j \bigr) v_i \Bigr) \\
   638	                   & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \alpha_i v_i \Bigr)\;,
   639	  \end{align*}
   640	  where we define $\alpha_i = \sum_j \alpha_{i, j} e_j$.
   641	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a bijection, this implies that $z = \sum_i
   642	  \alpha_i v_i$, and therefore $z^V = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i v_i$ (and similarly
   643	  $z^W = \sum_{i=m+1}^n \alpha_i v_i$).
   644	  This implies that
   645	  \begin{equation*}
   646		  \downsize_q(z)^{V'} = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j} \alpha_{i, j}
   647	    \downsize_q(e_j v_i) = \downsize_q (z^V)\;,
   648	  \end{equation*}
   649	  and similarly $\downsize_q(z)^{W'} = \downsize_q(z^W)$.
   650	  This completes the proof of the lemma.
   651	\end{proof}

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.
   751	  It cannot be the case that $\tr(e_i) = 0$ for all $i$.
   752	  Suppose that this were the case.
   753	  This would imply that $\tr(b) = 0$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   754	  But then for all $j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ and for some $b \neq 0$, we would
   755	  also have by item 1 of \Cref{lem:downsize_field} that $b_j = \tr(b e_j) = 0$ where $b = \sum_j b_j e_j$ with $b_j \in
   756	  \F_2$.
   757	  This implies that $b$ is the all zero element of $\F_{2^k}$, which is a
   758	  contradiction.
   759	  Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i=1, 2, \ldots, k$.
   760	
   761		The ``furthermore'' part follows item 1 of
   762	        \Cref{lem:downsize_field}:
   763	        \begin{equation*}
   764	          \downsize(1) = (\tr(1 \cdot e_1), \dots, \tr(1 \cdot e_k))
   765	          = (1, \dots, 1).
   766	        \end{equation*}
   767	\end{proof}
   768	
   769	\begin{lemma}
   770	  \label{lem:efficient_arithmetic}
   771	  For any odd integer $k$, let $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ denote the self-dual normal basis
   772	  of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ that is returned by the algorithm specified in
   773	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} on input $k$.
   774	  Then the following can be computed in time $\poly(k)$ on input $k$:
   775	  \begin{enumerate}
   776	  \item The representation $\downsize(a+b)$ of the sum $a+b$ given the
   777	    representations $\downsize(a)$ and $\downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$.

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}
  1127	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F^k$. For all $v \not\in V^\perp$, 
  1128	  \begin{equation*}

  1135	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single}
  1136	  \E_{a\in \F_q} \omega^{-\tr(ab)} \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b'\in \F_q} \E_{a\in \F_q}

  1138	\end{equation}
  1139	where the second step follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}.

  1142	$\qp^W$.

  1157	  \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b \in \Fq^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}

  1159	    \E_{a\in \F_q^n} \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)} \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b'\in \F_q^n} \E_{a\in \F_q^n}

  1161	\end{align}

     3	/-! # Structure and direct sums of conditionally linear functions
     4	
     5	This module records the prefix decomposition of a conditionally linear map and
     6	the behavior of such maps and their shared-seed distributions under finite
     7	coordinate direct sums.
     8	
     9	## References
    10	
    11	The source results are `lem:cl-kth`, `lem:cl-func-prod`, and
    12	`lem:cl-dist-prod` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:474-534`, with
    13	paper origin
    14	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:150-364`.
    15	-/
    16	
    17	open scoped BigOperators
    18	
    19	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    20	
    21	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    22	
    23	/-- The value of the strict-prefix marginal preceding `k`. This is a
    24	formalization-only auxiliary for `lem:cl-kth`, blueprint
    25	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:474-490`, paper
    26	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:150-178`. -/
    27	def clPrefix {K ι : Type*} [Zero K] {ell : ℕ}
    28	    (marginal : Fin ell → (ι → K) → (ι → K)) (k : Fin ell)
    29	    (x : ι → K) : ι → K :=
    30	  if _hk : k.val = 0 then 0
    31	  else marginal ⟨k.val - 1, lt_of_le_of_lt (Nat.sub_le _ _) k.isLt⟩ x
    32	
    33	/-- Prefix-indexed decomposition data from `lem:cl-kth`. Factor spaces are
    34	represented by their coordinate sets, matching the register-subspace encoding
    35	used by `IsCondLinearOn`. Blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:474-490`, paper
    36	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:150-178`. -/
    37	structure CLData (K ι : Type*) [Field K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    38	    (ell : ℕ) (L : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) where
    39	  /-- The marginal `L_{≤k}`. -/
    40	  marginal : Fin ell → (ι → K) → (ι → K)
    41	  /-- The factor register selected by a prefix value. -/
    42	  factor : Fin ell → (ι → K) → Finset ι
    43	  /-- The linear map selected by a prefix value. -/
    44	  linear : Fin ell → (ι → K) → ((ι → K) →ₗ[K] (ι → K))
    45	  /-- Each marginal has the corresponding conditionally linear level. -/
    46	  marginal_cl : ∀ k, IsCondLinearOn K Finset.univ (k.val + 1) (marginal k)
    47	  /-- The selected factor registers are pairwise disjoint. -/
    48	  factor_disjoint : ∀ x i j, i ≠ j →
    49	    Disjoint (factor i (clPrefix marginal i x)) (factor j (clPrefix marginal j x))
    50	  /-- The selected factor registers cover all coordinates. -/
    51	  factor_cover : ∀ x a, ∃ i, a ∈ factor i (clPrefix marginal i x)
    52	  /-- Each selected linear map is supported on its factor register. -/
    53	  linear_supported : ∀ k u x a, a ∉ factor k u → linear k u x a = 0
    54	  /-- Each marginal is the sum of the preceding selected linear pieces. -/
    55	  sum_formula : ∀ k x, marginal k x =
    56	    ∑ i : Fin ell, if i.val ≤ k.val then
    57	      linear i (clPrefix marginal i x)
    58	        (coordinateRestriction (factor i (clPrefix marginal i x)) x) else 0
    59	  /-- The final marginal is the original function. -/
    60	  top : ∀ h : 0 < ell,
    61	    marginal ⟨ell - 1, Nat.sub_lt h (by decide)⟩ = L
    62	
    63	/-- A map is `ell`-level conditionally linear exactly when it admits the
    64	prefix decomposition of `lem:cl-kth`; blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:474-494`,
    65	paper `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:150-262`. -/

    67	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] {ell : ℕ} (hEll : 1 ≤ ell)
    68	    (L : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) :
    69	    IsCondLinear ell L ↔ Nonempty (CLData K ι ell L) := by
    70	  sorry
    71	
    72	/-- Coordinate direct sum of maps supported on a finite register partition.
    73	This is a formalization-only auxiliary for `lem:cl-func-prod`, blueprint
    74	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:515-526`, paper
    75	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364`. -/
    76	def condLinearDirectSum {K ι : Type*} [Field K] [DecidableEq ι] {m : ℕ}
    77	    (V : Fin m → Finset ι) (L : Fin m → (ι → K) → (ι → K))

    95	    (hDisjoint : ∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (V i) (V j))

    97	    (hL : ∀ j, IsCondLinearOn K (V j) (ell j) (L j)) :
    98	    IsCondLinear (directSumLevel ell) (condLinearDirectSum V L) := by
    99	  sorry

   111	    (hDisjoint : ∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (V i) (V j))

1	\section{Conditionally Linear Functions, Distributions, and Samplers}
     2	\label{sec:linear}
     3	
     4	\subsection{Conditionally linear functions and distributions}
     5	\label{sec:cl}
     6	
     7	We first introduce \emph{conditionally linear functions}, which are used to
     8	specify the question distribution for games considered in the paper in a way
     9	that the question distribution can be ``introspected'', as described in
    10	Section~\ref{sec:introspection}.
    11	Intuitively, a conditionally linear function takes as input an element
    12	$x\in V = \F^n$ for some $n\geq 0$, and applies linear maps $L_j$ sequentially
    13	on $x^{V_j}$ where $V_1,V_2,\ldots $ are a sequence of complementary register
    14	subspaces such that both the linear maps $L_j$ and the subspace $V_j$ for
    15	$j \ge 2$ may depend on the values taken by previous linear maps $L_1(x^{V_1})$,
    16	$L_2(x^{V_2})$, etc.
    17	
    18	In the remainder of the section we use $V$ to denote the linear space $\F^n$ for
    19	some integer $n \geq 0$.
    20	For ease of notation we extensively use the subscript range notation.
    21	For example, if $V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_\ell$ are fixed subspaces of $V$ and $k \in
    22	\{1, 2, \ldots, \ell\}$ we write
    23	\begin{equation*}
    24	  V_{<k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,1 \le j<k} V_j\;,\quad
    25	  V_{> k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\, \ell\ge j > k} V_j\;,
    26	\end{equation*}
    27	and it is understood that $V_{\le k}$ and $V_{\ge k}$ are identical to
    28	$V_{<k+1}$ and $V_{>k-1}$, respectively.
    29	Moreover, if $V'$ is a register subspace of $V$, $F: V' \to V'$ is a function,
    30	and $x \in V$, we write $x^F$ to denote $F(x^{V'})$.
    31	For example, in the following definition $x^{L_1}$ is used as shorthand notation
    32	for $L_1(x^{V_1})$.
    33	
    34	
    35	\begin{definition}
    36	  \label{def:cl-func}
    37		Let $V$ be $\F^n$ for some $n\geq 0$.
    38	  For all integers $\ell\geq 0$ the collection of \emph{$\ell$-level
    39	    conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is defined
    40	  inductively as follows.
    41	  \begin{enumerate}
    42	  \item There is a single $0$-level conditionally linear function, which is the
    43	    $0$ function on $V$.
    44	
    45	  \item Let $\ell \geq 1$ and suppose the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level
    46	    conditionally linear functions has been defined.
    47	    The collection of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions on $V$ consists
    48	    of all functions $L$ on $V$ that can be expressed in the following form.
    49	    There exist complementary register subspaces $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ of $V$, a
    50	    linear function $L_1$ on $V_1$, and for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$, an
    51	    $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear function $L_{>1,\, v}$ on $V_{>1}$,
    52	    such that for all $x\in V$,
    53	    \begin{equation*}
    54	      L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}} (x^{V_{>1}})\;.
    55	    \end{equation*}
    56	  \end{enumerate}
    57	\end{definition}
    58	
    59	The concept of conditionally linear functions is simple even though the
    60	notations seem complicated.
    61	It is best understood using an operational definition illustrated in
    62	\cref{fig:cl-functions}.
    63	We give an example of a $2$-level CL function in \cref{ex:cl-function}.
    64	
    65	\begin{remark}
    66	  \label{rk:level-1-is-linear}
    67	  It follows from the above definition that all $1$-level CL functions are linear.
    68	\end{remark}
    69	
    70	\begin{example}\label{ex:cl-function}
    71	Consider $V = \F_{2}^{3}$. Then the following map
    72	\begin{equation*}
    73	  L:(x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2})
    74	  \mapsto (0, x_{0}x_{2} + x_{1}x_{2} + x_{0},  x_{2})
    75	\end{equation*}
    76	on $V$ is a $2$-level CL function by choosing $V_{1} = \mathrm{span}\{(0,0,1)\}$, $L_{1}$
    77	the identity function on $V_{1}$, $V_{2} = V_{1}^{\perp}$, and
    78	\begin{equation*}
    79	  L_{2,\, x_{2}}: (x_{0}, x_{1}, 0)
    80	  \mapsto (0, x_{0}x_{2} + x_{1}x_{2} + x_{0}, 0),
    81	\end{equation*}
    82	which is linear for all $x_{2} \in \F_{2}$.
    83	Note that intuitively the function $L$ selects either $x_{0}$ or $x_{1}$ in the
    84	second coordinate conditioning on the value of $x_{2}$.
    85	\end{example}
    86
