   275	We note that the marginal functions, factor spaces, and linear maps of a given
   276	CL function $L$ may not be unique; for example, consider the identity function
   277	on a linear space $V = \F^n$.
   278	This is clearly a $1$-level CL function, but it can also be viewed as a
   279	$k$-level CL function for $k \in \{2, \ldots, n\}$ with an arbitrary partition
   280	of $V$ into factor spaces.
   281	
   282	\begin{lemma}
   283	  \label{lem:cl-concat}
   284	  Let $\ell, k \ge 0$ be integers and $U = \F^n$, $V = \F^m$ be linear spaces.
   285	  Suppose $L$ is a $k$-level CL function on $U$ and $R_u$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   286	  function on $V$ for each $u \in L(U)$.
   287	  Then the \emph{concatenation} $T$ of $L$ and $\{R_u\}_u$ defined as
   288	  \begin{equation*}
   289	    T (x) = L(x^U) + R_{L(x^U)} (x^V)
   290	  \end{equation*}
   291	  is a $(k+\ell)$-level conditionally linear function on $U\oplus V$.
   292	\end{lemma}
   293	
   294	\begin{proof}
   295	  We prove the claim by induction on $k$.
   296	  The case $k = 0$ follows from the Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   297	  Assume that the lemma holds for $L$ being at most $(k-1)$-level.
   298	  By Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}, there are complementary register subspaces
   299	  $U_1$ and $U_{>1}$ of $U$, a linear function $L_1$ on $U_1$, and a family of
   300	  $(k-1)$-level CL functions $L_{>1,\, v}$ for $v \in L_1(U_1)$ such that
   301	  \begin{equation*}
   302	    L(x^U) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}).
   303	  \end{equation*}
   304	  For all $x^{L_1}$, define the function $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ on $U_{>1} \oplus V$ as
   305	  \begin{equation*}
   306	    T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1} \oplus V}) = L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}) +
   307	    R_{x^{L_1} + x^{L_{>1}}}(x^V),
   308	  \end{equation*}
   309	  the concatenation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ and $\{ R_{L(x^U)} \}_{x^{L_{>1}}}$
   310	  where $L_{>1}$ is the shorthand notation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$.
   311	  By the induction hypothesis, $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ is $(k+\ell-1)$-level
   312	  conditionally linear.
   313	  The lemma follows from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   314	\end{proof}
   315	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums of CL functions]
   316	  \label{lem:cl-func-prod}
   317	  Let $V^{(1)}, V^{(2)}, \ldots, V^{(m)}$ be register subspaces of $V$ such that
   318	  $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   319	  Suppose that, for each $j\in\{1, 2, \ldots, m\}$, $L^{(j)}$ is an
   320	  $\ell_j$-level conditionally linear function on $V^{(j)}$.
   321	  Then the direct sum $L = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   322	  function over $V$ for $\ell = \max_j \{\ell_j\}$, where $L$ is defined by
   323	  \begin{equation*}
   324	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m  L^{(j)}(x^{(j)})
   325	  \end{equation*}
   326	  for all $x = \sum_{j=1}^m x^{(j)} \in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   327	\end{lemma}
   328	
   329	\begin{proof}
   330	  It is easy to see that an $\ell$-level CL function is also $k$-level
   331	  conditionally linear for all $k \ge \ell$.
   332	  Hence, it suffices to prove the claim where $\ell_j = \ell$ for $j=1, 2,
   333	  \ldots, m$.
   334	
   335	  We prove the theorem by an induction on $\ell$.
   336	  For $\ell = 1$, the functions $L^{(j)}$ are linear and the claim follows by
   337	  the fact that the direct sum of linear maps is linear.
   338	
   339	  Assume now the theorem holds for conditionally linear functions of level at
   340	  most $\ell-1$ and $L^{(j)}$ are $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions
   341	  for $j=1, 2, ,\ldots, m$.
   342	  By definition, $L^{(j)}$ is the concatenation of conditionally linear
   343	  functions $L^{(j)}_{1}$ on $V^{(j)}_1$ and $\{ L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j} \}_{v_j}$
   344	  on $V^{(j)}_{>1}$ of levels $1$, and $\ell-1$ respectively.
   345	  Furthermore,
   346	  \begin{equation*}
   347	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)} (x^{(j)}) = \sum_{j=1}^m \Bigl( v_j +
   348	    L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   349	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr) \Bigr),
   350	  \end{equation*}
   351	  where $v_j = L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   352	    \Bigr)$.
   353	  By the induction hypothesis,
   354	  \begin{equation*}
   355	    L_{1} (x^{V_1}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   356	    \Bigr),\quad L_{>1,\, v} (x^{V_{>1}}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   357	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr)
   358	  \end{equation*}
   359	  are $1$-level and $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear respectively for $v =
   360	  \sum_j v_j$, $V_1 = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_1$, and $V_{>1} =
   361	  \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_{>1}$.
   362	  This proves that $L$ is $\ell$-level conditionally linear.
   363	\end{proof}
   364	
   365	\begin{lemma}
   366	  \label{lem:cl-dist-prod}
   367	  For each $i \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $L^{(i)}, R^{(i)} : V^{(i)} \to V^{(i)}$
   368	  be $\ell_i$-level conditionally linear functions and let $L, R: V \to V$ be the
   369	  direct sums $L = \bigoplus_i L_i$ and $R = \bigoplus_i R_i$, respectively, as
   370	  defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}.
   371	  Then the conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L, R}$ is the product
   372	  distribution $\prod_{i=1}^m \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ over $V \times V$.
   373	\end{lemma}
   374	
   375	\begin{proof}
   376		The distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ is the distribution over pairs $(L(x),R(x))$
   377	  where $x$ is sampled uniformly from $V \times V$.
   378	  By Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}, this is equivalent to the distribution over
   379	  pairs $\bigl( (L_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m, (R_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m \bigr)$ where $x$
   380	  is chosen uniformly at random from $V$.
   381	  This distribution is exactly the product of the distributions $
   382	  \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, m$.
   383	\end{proof}

68	\begin{definition}[Projective strategies]
    69	  \label{def:projective-strategy}
    70	  We say that a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ is \emph{projective} if
    71	  all the measurements $\{A^x_a\}_a$ and $\{B^y_b\}_b$ are projective.
    72	\end{definition}
    73	
    74	\begin{definition}\label{rem:symmetric-games}
    75		A game $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is
    76	  \emph{symmetric} if the question and answer alphabets are the same for both
    77	  players (i.e.\
    78	  $\cal{X} = \cal{Y}$ and $\cal{A} = \cal{B}$), the distribution $\mu$ is
    79	  symmetric (i.e.\
    80	  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y,x)$), and the decision predicate $D$ treats both players
    81	  symmetrically (i.e.\ for all $x,y,a,b$, $D(x,y,a,b) = D(y,x,b,a)$).
    82	 
    83	We call a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$
    84	  \emph{symmetric} if $\ket{\psi}$ is a (pure) state in $\mH \otimes \mH$, for some
    85	  Hilbert space $\mH$, that is invariant under permutation of the two factors,
    86	  and the measurement operators of both players are identical.
    87	\end{definition}
    88	
    89	We often specify symmetric games $\game$ and symmetric strategies $\strategy$ using
    90	  a compact notation: we write $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A}, \mu, D)$ and
    91	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ where $M$ denotes the set of measurement
    92	  operators for both players.
    93	
    94	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:symmetric-strat}
    95	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A},  \mu, D)$ be a symmetric game
    96	  such that $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$ for some $\eps\geq 0$.
    97	  Then there exists a symmetric and projective strategy
    98	  $\strategy=(\ket{\psi},M)$ such that $\val^*(\game,\strategy)\geq 1-\eps$.
    99	\end{lemma}
   100	
   101	\begin{proof}
   102	  By definition for any $\eps'>\eps$ there exists a strategy $\strategy'= (\ket{\psi'},A,B)$ such
   103	  that $\val^*(\game,\strategy')\geq 1-\eps'$.
   104	Using Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}) we can assume
   105	without loss of generality that $\ket{\psi'}\in\C_{\alice'}^d\otimes \C_{\bob'}^d$ for some integer $d$
   106	  and that for every $x$, $A^x$ and $B^x$ are projective measurements.
   107	Let
   108	  \[
   109	    \ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big( \ket{0}_\alice \ket{1}_\bob
   110	    \ket{\psi'}_{\alice'\bob'} + \ket{1}_\alice \ket{0}_\bob
   111	    \ket{\psi'_\tau}_{\alice'\bob'}\big) \in (\C_{\alice}^2 \otimes
   112	    \C_{\alice'}^d) \otimes (\C_\bob^2 \otimes \C_{\bob'}^d)\;,
   113	  \]
   114	  where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ is obtained from $\ket{\psi}$ by permuting the two
   115	  players' registers.
   116	  Observe that $\ket{\psi}$ is invariant under permutation of $\alice\alice'$
   117	  and $\bob\bob'$.
   118	
   119	  For any question $x\in \cal{X}$ define the measurement $M^x = \{M^x_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$
   120	  acting on the Hilbert space $\C^2 \otimes \C^d$ as follows:
   121	  \[
   122	  	M^x_a = \ketbra{0}{0} \otimes A^x_a + \ketbra{1}{1} \otimes B^x_a \;,
   123	  \]
   124		i.e.\ for $\ket{\varphi} \in \C^d$, $M^x_a(\ket{0}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{0}A^x_a\ket{\varphi}$ and $M^x_a(\ket{1}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{1}B^x_a\ket{\varphi}$.
   125	  When Alice receives question $x$, she measures $M^x$ on registers $\alice \alice'$, and when Bob receives 
   126	  question $y$, he measures $M^y$ on registers $\bob \bob'$.
   127	Using that by assumption the decision predicate $D$ for $\game$ is symmetric,
   128	  it is not hard to verify that $\val^*(\game,\strategy) =
   129	  \val^*(\game,\strategy')$.
   130	\end{proof}

   120		Let $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal A, \mu, D)$ be a symmetric game such that $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G) = 1-\eps$ for some $\eps \ge 0$. Then there exists a symmetric and projective strategy $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ such that $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) \ge 1-\eps$.
   121	\end{lemma}
   122	\begin{proof}
   123		\uses{thm:naimark}
   124		The symmetrization argument establishes the following approximate form of the conclusion: for every $\eps' > \eps$ there exists a symmetric and projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps'$. Indeed, fix $\eps' > \eps$. Since $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G)$ is the supremum of the values of all strategies, there exists a strategy $\mathcal S' = (\ket{\psi'}, A, B)$ with $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S') \ge 1-\eps'$. Using Naimark dilation (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}), each dilated sub-measurement being completed to a projective measurement by assigning to one fixed outcome the residual projector of its family --- which changes no correlation on the extended state, as described in Remark~\ref{rem:naimark-for-games} above --- we may assume without loss of generality that $\ket{\psi'} \in \C^d_{A'} \ot \C^d_{B'}$ for some integer $d$ and that every $A^x$ and $B^x$ is a projective measurement. Let
   125		\[
   126			\ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\, \bigl( \ket{0}_{A}\ket{1}_{B}\ket{\psi'}_{A'B'} + \ket{1}_{A}\ket{0}_{B}\ket{\psi'_\tau}_{A'B'} \bigr) \in \bigl(\C^2_{A} \ot \C^d_{A'}\bigr) \ot \bigl(\C^2_{B} \ot \C^d_{B'}\bigr)\,,
   127		\]
   128		where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ is obtained from $\ket{\psi'}$ by permuting the two players' registers; then $\ket{\psi}$ is invariant under permutation of the register pairs $AA'$ and $BB'$. For each question $x \in \mathcal X$ define the projective measurement $M^x = \{M^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ on $\C^2 \ot \C^d$ by
   129		\[
   130			M^x_a = \ket{0}\bra{0} \ot A^x_a + \ket{1}\bra{1} \ot B^x_a\,,
   131		\]
   132		and let each player measure $M$ on their pair of registers. Because the decision predicate $D$ of the symmetric game treats the two players symmetrically, the resulting symmetric projective strategy $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ satisfies $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) = \operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S') \ge 1-\eps'$. Note that this construction preserves the value of the strategy it is applied to exactly.
   133	
   134		The statement asserts more, namely a single symmetric projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps$ itself. Passing from the family of strategies constructed above to one attaining the bound $1-\eps$ is an attainment step which the argument does not supply: the supremum defining $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G)$ in Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-value} ranges over strategies of unbounded dimension and need not be attained. This step remains unproved; the obstruction, and the forms of the lemma that the argument does prove, are documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_symmetrization-attainment}. See also Remark~\ref{rem:symmetric-strat-limit}.
   135	\end{proof}
   136	
   137	\begin{remark}[Attainment in the symmetrization lemma]\label{rem:symmetric-strat-limit}
   138		The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-strat} yields, for each $\eps' > \eps$, a symmetric projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps'$. The conclusion as stated, at $\eps' = \eps$, does not follow from this: the dilated dimension $d$ may grow as $\eps' \downarrow \eps$, and the supremum defining $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G)$ in Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-value} need not be attained by any strategy. The symmetrization construction itself is value-preserving, so the conclusion does hold whenever the hypothesis supplies an actual strategy of value at least $1-\eps$ rather than only the value of the game; every use of the lemma in the source proceeds from such a strategy, or from a strict lower bound on the value, and therefore consumes only what the proof establishes. The gap and the available repairs are documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_symmetrization-attainment}.
   139	\end{remark}

   113	\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}
   114		The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.
   115	\end{remark}

/-- The coefficient-tuple answer alphabet of the low-degree game.  Polynomial

inductive LdAnswer (P : LdParams) where
  | pointVals (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P)
  | alinePolys (a : Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
  | dlinePolys (a : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
  deriving DecidableEq

/-- A finite sum code used only to provide the answer alphabet's `Fintype`
instance; the public constructors are those of `def:ld-win-predicate`,
blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
abbrev LdAnswerCode (P : LdParams) :=
  (Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) ⊕
    ((Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P) ⊕
      (Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P))

/-- The constructor-preserving code equivalence for `LdAnswer` (Lean-only
finite-carrier infrastructure for `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
-/
noncomputable def ldAnswerEquiv (P : LdParams) :
    LdAnswer P ≃ LdAnswerCode P where
  toFun
    | .pointVals a => .inl a
    | .alinePolys a => .inr (.inl a)
    | .dlinePolys a => .inr (.inr a)
  invFun
    | .inl a => .pointVals a
    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePolys a
    | .inr (.inr a) => .dlinePolys a
  left_inv := by intro x; cases x <;> rfl
  right_inv := by
    intro x
    cases x with
    | inl a => rfl
    | inr x =>
        cases x with
        | inl a => rfl
        | inr a => rfl

instance (P : LdParams) : Inhabited (LdAnswer P) :=
  ⟨.pointVals (fun _ => 0)⟩

noncomputable instance (P : LdParams) : Fintype (LdAnswer P) :=
  Fintype.ofEquiv (LdAnswerCode P) (ldAnswerEquiv P).symm

/-- Evaluation of a coefficient tuple at a field element.  This is the
representative convention used by the line answers in `def:ld-win-predicate`,
blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
def evalCoefficient {K : Type*} [Semiring K] {n : ℕ}
    (c : Fin n → K) (t : K) : K :=
  ∑ i : Fin n, c i * t ^ i.val

/-- Check that an answer has the constructor prescribed by its question type;
Lean encoding of the rejection clause in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
def validLdAnswer {P : LdParams} (t : LdType) (a : LdAnswer P) : Bool :=
  match t, a with
  | .point, .pointVals _ => true
  | .aline, .alinePolys _ => true
  | .dline, .dlinePolys _ => true
  | _, _ => false

/-- The axis-parallel line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
def alinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
  -- Universal quantification follows the zero-direction convention in
  -- `rem:ld-win-zero-direction`.
  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
    point.point = line.point + t • coordinateDirection (chiIndex P line.seed) →
      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j

/-- The diagonal line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
def dlinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
    point.point = line.point + t • line.direction →
      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j

/-- The low-degree consistency predicate, rejecting answers of the wrong
constructor shape.  This is `def:ld-win-predicate` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

noncomputable def ldWinPredicate (P : LdParams) :
    LdQuestion P → LdQuestion P → LdAnswer P → LdAnswer P → Bool :=
  open Classical in
  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
      if validLdAnswer tA a && validLdAnswer tB b then
        match tA, tB, a, b with
        | .point, .point, .pointVals u, .pointVals v => decide (u = v)
        | .aline, .point, .alinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
            decide (alinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
        | .point, .aline, .pointVals u, .alinePolys f =>
            decide (alinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
        | .dline, .point, .dlinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
            decide (dlinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
        | .point, .dline, .pointVals u, .dlinePolys f =>
            decide (dlinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
        | .aline, .aline, .alinePolys f, .alinePolys g => decide (f = g)
        | .dline, .dline, .dlinePolys f, .dlinePolys g => decide (f = g)

  QuestionA := LdQuestion P
  QuestionB := LdQuestion P
  AnswerA := LdAnswer P
  AnswerB := LdAnswer P
  μ := ldQuestionDistribution P
  μ_prob := by sorry
  decide := ldWinPredicate P

   214	  | pointVals (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P)

   216	  | dlinePolys (a : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)

   232	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).

   235	    LdAnswer P ≃ LdAnswerCode P where
   236	  toFun
   237	    | .pointVals a => .inl a
   238	    | .alinePolys a => .inr (.inl a)
   239	    | .dlinePolys a => .inr (.inr a)
   240	  invFun
   241	    | .inl a => .pointVals a
   242	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePolys a
   243	    | .inr (.inr a) => .dlinePolys a
   244	  left_inv := by intro x; cases x <;> rfl
   245	  right_inv := by
   246	    intro x
   247	    cases x with
   248	    | inl a => rfl
   249	    | inr x =>
   250	        cases x with
   251	        | inl a => rfl
   252	        | inr a => rfl

   301	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,

   326	        | .dline, .dline, .dlinePolys f, .dlinePolys g => decide (f = g)

A two-outcome projective measurement is consistent on a state if and only if its observable $\mathcal O$ satisfies $\mathcal O \ot I \ket{\psi} = I \ot \mathcal O \ket{\psi}$; since $A$ and $B$ are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot n}$ by hypothesis and $\sigma^X$, $\sigma^Z$ are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$, each cell observable is a product of consistent, commuting factors and is therefore consistent on $\ket{\psi}$, and consistency of the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ measurements follows from the cellwise consistencies together with commutativity. Together with consistency this shows that every check of the Magic Square game is passed with probability $1$, so the strategy has value $1$.
